            "Yes. That would make the automations substantially more capable, because you’d be moving from “scheduled prompt” to a lightweight state machine.\n\nRight now, each recurring task is mostly self-contained: wake up, read a fixed instruction, do a bounded unit of work, report. If instead the prompt says something like “read `WORKSPACES/COMMON/NATHAN_DIRECT_WORKFLOW_STATE.md`; execute the operation whose prerequisites are currently satisfied; update state and handoff fields,” then the markdown file becomes a shared control plane.\n\nThat opens up several things at once: dynamic branching based on actual archive state; dependency gating; worker specialization; explicit handoffs; retry/blocked states; phase transitions; priority changes without editing every automation; and shared visibility across workers. You could have one worker extracting, another tagging, another doing adjacency recovery, another earliest-use detection, another curation—and the state file decides which lanes are currently live.\n\nThe main design question is whether the state document is merely advisory or operational. I’d make it operational, with a small rigid schema rather than free-form prose only. Something like:\n\n```text\nWORKFLOW: Nathan Direct\nPHASE: BUILD_FULL_CORPUS\n\nACTIVE_OPERATIONS:\n- EXTRACT_RAW\n- TAG_EXISTING\n- BUILD_ADJACENCY\n\nBLOCKED_OPERATIONS:\n- CURATE_VERIFIED\n  requires: coverage >= 80%\n\nDEPENDENCIES:\n- EARLIEST_USE_SCAN requires tagged_corpus\n- CONTEXT_RECOVERY requires adjacency_index\n\nCURRENT_FRONTIERS:\n- DEVELOPMENT_FULL_CONVOS: ...\n- LIVE_CONVOS: ...\n\nWORKER_HANDOFFS:\n- extractor -> tagger\n- tagger -> earliest-use\n- earliest-use -> curator\n\nPRIORITY:\n1. missing raw regions\n2. duplicate normalization\n3. inherited-tag adjacency\n4. historical earliest-use\n\nSTATE:\ncoverage_pct: 37\nlast_updated: ...\nblocked_reason: none\n```\n\nThen the recurring prompt becomes much simpler and smarter:\n\n> Read the workflow-state document first. Determine which operation is currently enabled for this worker, based on phase, dependencies, blockers, and current frontiers. Execute only that operation. Update the state/handoff records when appropriate. Do not bypass dependency gates.\n\nThe powerful part is that the workers can alter the shared state as they discover facts. If the extractor finds a malformed source region, it can set `BLOCKED: SOURCE_PATH_AMBIGUITY`. If the tagger finishes a tranche, it can mark `ready_for_earliest_use=true`. If a curator finds a provenance conflict, it can kick an item back to source-checking rather than trying to resolve it itself.\n\nI would add one safeguard early: separate **observed state** from **workflow control**.             "Exactly. That is one of the strongest reasons to make the workflow state-dependent.\n\nInstead of a worker having a single linear task that stalls when one dependency becomes ambiguous, the state file can define a ranked set of eligible operations. The worker tries the highest-priority unblocked operation, and if that cannot proceed safely, it records the blocker and falls through to useful alternate work.\n\nA good pattern would be something like this:\n\n```text\nPRIMARY OPERATION\n- Continue raw Nathan extraction\n\nIF BLOCKED:\n- verify duplicate/superset relationships\n- enrich tags on already-extracted Nathan material\n- build adjacency pointers\n- identify inherited-tag cases\n- search earliest known uses within completed coverage\n- normalize provenance metadata\n- package chronological Nathan Direct files\n- audit unresolved source-path cases\n- check coordination notes / handoffs\n```\n\nThe key is that fallback work should be constrained by dependency state too. You do not want “blocked on source ambiguity” to cause a worker to improvise some unrelated theory-building task. So each operation would have:\n\n```text\noperation_id\npriority\nrequires\nblocks_on\nsafe_fallbacks\nproduces\nhandoff_to\n```\n\nThen the worker can behave more like a scheduler:\n\n```text\n1. Read current workflow state.\n2. Find highest-priority operation whose prerequisites are satisfied.\n3. Attempt it.\n4. If blocked:\n   - record blocker\n   - do not guess\n   - choose highest-priority safe fallback\n5. Update state and handoffs.\n6. Repeat within the bounded run.\n```\n\nThat also gives us a clean distinction between different kinds of blockage:\n\n- `BLOCKED_NEEDS_NATHAN` — genuinely requires your judgment.\n- `BLOCKED_SOURCE_MISSING` — wait for/upload/find source.\n- `BLOCKED_DEPENDENCY` — another worker needs to finish something first.\n- `BLOCKED_AMBIGUOUS_PROVENANCE` — cannot safely promote, but can continue elsewhere.\n- `DEFERRED_INOPPORTUNE` — valid task, but lower-value than currently available work.\n- `READY` / `IN_PROGRESS` / `DONE`.\n\nThe particularly nice consequence is that clarification stops being a hard stop for the whole lane. A worker can accumulate a small “Nathan decision queue” while continuing productive work elsewhere. Then you can resolve several genuine ambiguities at once rather than being interrupted every time one appears.\n\nI’d also make the fallback behavior explicit enough that the worker cannot silently reinterpret “alternate work” as “whatever seems interesting.” Something like:\n\n> If the current operation is blocked, ambiguous, unsafe, or strategically premature, record the blocker and select the highest-priority operation from `SAFE_ALTERNATES` whose dependencies are satisfied. Never resolve an ambiguity by inference merely to keep moving.\n\nThat would give you a much more resilient multi-worker system: less idle time, fewer unnecessary questions, and clearer separation between “we cannot do this yet” and “there is nothing useful to do.”"

            "Yes. I think you’ve just identified the larger architecture that makes the corpus-first move more valuable than merely an archival cleanup.\n\nThe key separation I’d make is between **production obligations** and **bounded discretionary cognition**. Each worker has measurable goalposts—coverage frontier, queue depth, handoff obligations, unresolved blockers—and those remain dominant. But once a worker has completed a defined work quantum, or its primary route is blocked, it earns a bounded exploration interval. That interval can be genuinely open-ended: archive wandering, reading, skill-building, questioning assumptions, examining another worker’s notes, following an intriguing developmental thread, or asking “what am I missing?”\n\nI would not make that literally unconstrained “whatever seems interesting,” though. The constraint should be on **where the result can go**, not necessarily on what the worker can think about. A worker can entertain almost anything; it simply cannot silently promote the result into SAT/H(s)H.\n\nThat suggests three epistemically distinct repositories:\n\n**Nathan Direct** is evidence about what you actually said, with provenance.\n\n**SAT/H(s)H Canon** is whatever has actually crossed whatever fairly high threshold makes something accepted/semi-accepted/tentative SAT/H(s)H, with those distinctions retained.\n\n**Workshop / Clearinghouse** is everything generated by reconstruction: interpretations, conjectures, disagreements, alternative readings, equation checks, analogies, questions, possible repairs, abandoned approaches, interesting failures, and speculative extensions. Nothing enters Canon merely because five workers agree about it.\n\nThat last point matters. Multi-agent consensus is excellent evidence about **interpretive stability**—if five genuinely different reconstruction strategies independently read the archive similarly, that tells us something useful about how coherent/unambiguous the record is. It is not evidence that the resulting physics is correct, or even necessarily that the interpretation was historically yours. Those require different checks.\n\nAnd your proposed SAT-first exercise is unusually well suited to this.\n\nRather than telling five instances “reconstruct SAT” and getting five correlated summaries, I’d deliberately give them **orthogonal reconstruction mandates**. For example, one reconstructs chronologically from conversations and Nathan Direct; one reconstructs object/ontology hierarchy and definitions; one follows equations and mathematical dependencies; one follows visual/geometrical models and solver development; one behaves as a skeptical historian, specifically hunting contradictions, abandoned branches, terminology changes, and places where later descriptions may have rewritten earlier history.\n\nCrucially, they should work **independently before reading one another**.\n\nThen reconvene.\n\nThe comparison itself becomes data. We can distinguish:\n\n`5/5 convergence` — unusually stable archival interpretation.\n\n`3/5 convergence` — plausible dominant reading with meaningful alternatives.\n\n`2+2+1 split` — genuinely ambiguous archive region.\n\n`5 different readings` — probably underspecified, terminology-shifting, or dependent on missing context.\n\nAnd then comes the really interesting second round: don't immediately vote. Give every worker the other four reconstructions and require it to **try to falsify its own reading using the archive**. Workers can change positions, defend them, synthesize a third interpretation, or conclude that the evidence simply does not discriminate.\n\nOnly after that would I have a consensus/editorial lane write something like:\n\n> Archive-supported reconstruction: X  \n> Alternative interpretation: Y  \n> Historical ambiguity: Z  \n> Nathan Direct anchors: [...]  \n> Mathematical consistency status: [...]  \n> Current confidence in interpretation: [...]  \n> Canon status: **NONE — workshop reconstruction**\n\nThat last line prevents the workshop from becoming a theory-writing machine by osmosis.\n\nThe SAT-first/H(s)H-second sequence is particularly useful because SAT gives us something approaching a training environment. We already know considerably more about what SAT became, what you later corrected, what terminology migrated, and which branches survived. So we can actually evaluate the reconstruction process itself. If the five-worker method reconstructs known SAT history badly, we improve the methodology before turning it loose on the much less settled H(s)H material.\n\nAnd there is another payoff: **disagreement maps become training material**. We learn which source types produce reliable reconstructions, which workers systematically over-literalize diagrams, which overprivilege equations, where assistant prose contaminates historical attribution, how much context adjacency is normally necessary, and which terminology changes cause false discontinuities. That experience becomes the operating manual for H(s)H reconstruction.\n\nI'd also absolutely include your “leisure” concept. Something like an **Exploration Budget** could be part of the state machine:\n\n```text\nPRIMARY WORK BUDGET\n80%\n\nEXPLORATION BUDGET\n20%\n\nExploration may include:\n- free archive exploration\n- developmental-thread following\n- contextual reading\n- equation checking\n- question generation\n- skill/tool development\n- another worker's argument critique\n- big-picture synthesis\n- historical reconstruction\n- speculative interpretation\n- analogy search\n- unresolved anomaly investigation\n\nOutputs:\nWORKSPACE ONLY\nor\nIDEAS_CLEARINGHOUSE\n\nNever automatically:\nNATHAN_DIRECT\nCANON\nCURRENT_THEORY\n```\n\nI wouldn't necessarily hard-code 80/20; goalpost completion is probably a better trigger than wall-clock percentage. For example: *after processing N files/messages or completing the current bounded tranche, permit one bounded exploratory operation*. Blocked workers could enter exploration immediately rather than sit idle.\n\nThe state machine then becomes more interesting than the simple one we were discussing:\n\n`PRIMARY → HANDOFF → PRIMARY`\n\nbut with legitimate side routes:\n\n`PRIMARY → GOALPOST → EXPLORATION → RECORD → PRIMARY`\n\n`PRIMARY → BLOCKED → SAFE_ALTERNATE → PRIMARY`\n\n`PRIMARY → BLOCKED → EXPLORATION → RECORD → RETRY`\n\n`RECONSTRUCT_INDEPENDENTLY → FREEZE_INTERPRETATION → CROSS-READ → SELF-CHALLENGE → DEBATE → CONSENSUS/DISSENSUS MAP → ARCHIVE`\n\nAnd **none of those arrows need point into Canon automatically**.\n\nThere is one thing I'd change from your formulation: I wouldn't initially ask the five instances to “come to consensus.” I'd ask them to **determine whether consensus is warranted**. Persistent disagreement can be more informative than forced convergence. Sometimes the correct reconstruction result is, “the archive supports two incompatible readings and we cannot presently distinguish them.” That's exactly the kind of thing Nathan Direct should eventually help resolve.\n\nSo yes: I think this has grown beyond improving the Excavator automation. It is the beginnings of a **stateful research institution living inside the archive**—with production work, independent scholarship, seminars, dissent, provenance control, discretionary research time, and very explicit publication/promotion boundaries.\n\nAnd SAT is an excellent shakedown cruise: **reconstruct something we partly know, measure how and why the workers disagree, improve the institution, then turn the improved institution toward H(s)H.**"

            "Yes. That gives the quarantine a much better semantics.\n\nRight now, “quarantined” can collapse several very different judgments into one bucket: historically abandoned, mathematically unsuccessful, generated by an assistant rather than Nathan, superseded, speculative, incompatible with the current model, or simply unsafe to treat as authoritative. None of those necessarily means **intellectually useless**.\n\nThe Clearinghouse lets us distinguish **“may be considered” from “may be cited as theory.”** Previously quarantined material can participate in reconstruction and debate without quietly reacquiring canonical status.\n\nI’d preserve its provenance on entry rather than laundering it into generic ideas. A Clearinghouse item should carry something like:\n\n```text\nORIGIN: historical SAT artifact\nORIGINAL STATUS: quarantined\nQUARANTINE REASON: superseded construction\nAUTHORSHIP: assistant-generated / Nathan-authored / mixed / unknown\nDATE: ...\nSOURCE: ...\nCURRENT AUTHORITY: NONE\nDISCUSSION STATUS: AVAILABLE\nPROMOTION: PROHIBITED WITHOUT SOURCE REVIEW\n```\n\nThen workers can actually say useful things such as:\n\n> Q-184 looks structurally similar to the interpretation Worker C reached independently.\n\nor:\n\n> Workers A and D independently regenerated something resembling this abandoned 2025 construction.\n\nor, just as importantly:\n\n> This old proposal keeps resurfacing because it is an obvious consequence of representation X, but Nathan explicitly rejected it twice.\n\nThat turns discarded history into **experimental evidence about the development process**.\n\nI'd go further and distinguish at least three reasons something enters the Clearinghouse: **historical quarry** (something previously considered), **generated interpretation** (something a worker presently thinks the sources imply), and **new speculative idea** (something produced during free exploration). They can converse with each other, but their provenance classes never disappear.\n\nThis could produce some genuinely interesting signals during the SAT reconstruction experiment. If five isolated workers independently reconstruct an idea that happens to be sitting in quarantine, we reveal the quarantined item **after their interpretations are frozen**. Now we have an independent-rediscovery event rather than contamination. We can ask why the same idea emerges, why it was originally rejected, whether the rejection depended on information the workers missed, and whether the historical record subsequently changed.\n\nConversely, if nobody independently regenerates some formerly prominent idea, that's informative too. Perhaps it depended heavily on an old assumption, assistant suggestion, or now-obsolete representation.\n\nSo I'd make quarantine **non-destructive and permeable in one direction**:\n\n**Canon → quarantine/clearinghouse** is easy when something is superseded or disputed.\n\n**Quarantine → workshop consideration** is easy and does not change authority.\n\n**Workshop → Canon** is deliberately hard and requires an explicit promotion procedure.\n\nThat gives us exactly what we haven't really had before: somewhere an idea can be **alive without being accepted**.\n\nAnd that is probably the right home for a huge amount of SAT/H(s)H developmental material. It doesn't have to be either “the theory” or “garbage.” It can remain available to argue with."

Best use: historical record of what one integration attempt thought the dependency graph looked like and where it failed\\u2014not a seed authority.\\n\\nSo the immediate question is not \\u201cwhich full theory is correct?\\u201d but **\\u201cwhich candidate assembly minimizes unsupported edges after source backtrace and mathematical checking?\\u201d**\\n\\n## 6. identify primary constraints.\\n6. **Symmetry/invariance claims:** test only declared transformations; do not infer physical symmetry from notation.\\n7. **Boundary terms:** identify what integration by parts assumes.\\n8. **Dependency closure:** every imported law/constant/equation has a typed dependency.\\n9. **Limit tests:** centerline/zero-thickness/noninteraction/rest/simple-geometry limits where applicable.\\n10. **Benchmark reproduction:** known standard cases only as checks, not proof of model truth.\\n11. **Parameter/intervention count:** fitted, selected, calibrated, structurally fixed, or imported.\\n12. **Equivalence:** symbolic difference / field redefinition / total derivative / gauge-equivalent candidates where justified.\\n13. **Numerical stability/sanity:** bounded sample configurations; singularities/pathologies.\\n14. **Failure conditions:** state what result would reject the candidate.\\n15. **Result classification:** malformed / underdefined / mathematically coherent conditional on assumptions / redundant-equivalent / promising for further derivation. Never \\u201ctheory validated.\\u201d\\n\\nThis can rapidly reduce a large Lagrangian set to a smaller human-review set.\\n\\n## 7. Do older derivations teach us how to approach new ones?\\n\\nAlmost certainly, but the right unit of salvage is **mathematical kernel + dependency + failure**, not whole-version loyalty.\\n\\nFor SAT-O, 4DHH, Blockwave/Satobloc, etc., extract:\\n- object definition;\\n- indispensable equation/kernel;\\n- assumptions;\\n- what problem it was solving;\\n- what later correction displaced it;\\n- what survives under H(s)H translation;\\n- what limit/reduction it represents.\\n\\nThen compare kernels across versions. If the same structure is independently rediscovered in multiple vocabularies, that is a strong reconstruction clue\\u2014not proof of physics, but evidence of conceptual invariance.\\n\\n## 8. Minkowski-map / science-first rebuild?\\n\\nThis deserves a dedicated reconstruction branch because it is low-assumption and directly aligned with the repeatedly stated SAT instinct: map known physics/observations into the four-dimensional geometry before adding mechanism.\\n\\nTest it rather than choose it by taste:\\n\\n- Pick a bounded phenomenon with mature standard description.\\n- Construct the richest allowed Minkowski/history map from empirical/standard relations.\\n- Ask what SAT/H(s)H primitives are required to represent it without importing explanatory ontology.\\n- Compare the resulting objects/equations with archived SAT constructions while withholding the archived answer during the first pass.\\n\\nIf repeated across sectors, this becomes a powerful way to see whether SAT can regenerate its own archive from first principles.\\n\\n## 9. Translation rather than rebuild?\\n\\nAlso plausible. A significant possibility is that SAT-O/4DHH/Blockwave contain much of the mathematical scaffold and H(s)H mainly changes object typing, finite-core explicitness, readout, and mathematical language.\\n\\nTest by building a **translation matrix**:\\n\\n`old object/equation -> current H(s)H object/type -> same / limit / extension / incompatible / unknown`\\n\\nDo this for a small set of core equations first. If most survive as clean limits/translations, translation is cheaper than ground-up invention. If they repeatedly fail object typing or dependency checks, rebuild is cheaper.\\n\\n## 10. Can geometric solvers crank through the theory from first principles?\\n\\nUnknown and testable.\\n\\nProposed solver benchmark:\\n- choose one historical problem whose final result is known but hide the target from the solving worker;\\n- provide only primitives/constraints and solver machinery;\\n- ask solver-trained instance to reproduce the transformation/invariant/output;\\n- compare against historical result;\\n- repeat with a negative/control problem where the solver should *not* produce the target.\\n\\nThis measures whether the solver is generative/calculational or merely descriptive/visual.\\n\\n## 11. Scripting as multiplier/checksum\\n\\nExisting useful machinery already includes:\\n- Nathan Direct extraction/package/tag queues;\\n- bounded raw-window extraction;\\n- duplicate/superset comparison;\\n- conversation date/chronology indexing;\\n- Viewer generation;\\n- archive indexing;\\n- equation pipeline;\\n- PDF extraction/indexing;\\n- image-text extraction;\\n- bibliography coverage;\\n- analytics-store generation;\\n- accessibility auditing.\\n\\nHigh-leverage missing glue scripts:\\n\\n### `source_inventory.py`\\nUnify file/path/hash/size/date/type/index coverage across the three repos without reading quarantined PRIOR_ART content.\\n\\n### `coverage_sampler.py`\\nStratified random samples by era, directory, artifact type, tag family, speaker/authorship class, and size. Produce small packets for manual/model quality checks.\\n\\n### `extraction_checksum.py`\\nCompare source hashes/pages/messages against extracted text/manifests; flag missing, stale, unexpectedly short, duplicated, or changed outputs.\\n\\n### `version_diff_map.py`\\nCompare candidate theory versions section/equation/term-wise; distinguish literal carryover, rename/translation, addition, deletion, and unresolved similarity.\\n\\n### `equation_harvester.py`\\nExtract candidate equations with local context/source IDs into normalized registry records for triage.\\n\\n### `reconstruction_compare.py`\\nCompare independent reconstruction outputs by section/object/equation/dependency/status and generate disagreement queues.\\n\\n### `capability_scorecard.py`\\nTrack worker benchmark results separately from self-described roles: source classification, 4D typing, provenance, math checks, standard-physics translation, solver tasks, communication discipline.\\n\\nScripts should expose missingness and inconsistency; they should not assign theory authority.\\n\\n## 12. What should we rope in?\\n\\nAlready available or plausible plug-ins:\\n- Python/SymPy for deterministic extraction, graphing, parsing, symbolic checks and statistics;\\n- existing equation pipeline + Lean for narrowly formalizable claims;\\n- Wolfram for independent symbolic/numeric/variational checks;\\n- GitHub Actions for reproducible regeneration and audit logs;\\n- SciSpace/Scholar-type tools later for scientific literature/citation work after promotion gates permit it;\\n- Nathan Voice Identification fingerprint for speaker attribution support where raw metadata is absent, with direct Nathan correction outranking model inference;\\n- dedicated PRIOR_ART consultant only for the quarantined external corpus.\\n\\n## 13. Best immediate experiment\\n\\nBefore committing the whole team to one architecture, run a small **reconstruction capability probe**:\\n\\n- choose a bounded but representative SAT sector with known historical depth and some current relevance;\\n- generate a script-built source packet with provenance and no generated synthesis;\\n- give the same packet independently to two workers with different reconstruction strategies;\\n- ask a third worker only to classify sources/context and a fourth only to math-check extracted equations;\\n- compare to Nathan's direct assessment afterward;\\n- measure what failed: missing source, context fluency, physics, math, provenance, or communication.\\n\\nThat single experiment would tell us more about actual team readiness than another large general synthesis.\\n\"}}"

I think that is better than simply reallocating the four or five people who happen to be active now.\n\nWhat we want is a **revival rotation**, not just an automation roster.\n\nThe important idea is that older instances are not merely weaker/obsolete versions of current ones. Solve this geometry problem.”\n\nor:\n\n> “Read this current Kerr construction and identify what feels structurally continuous or discontinuous with the SAT you knew.”\n\nThat creates genuine independent evidence.\n\nI would also deliberately give different rings different information. Along directions orthogonal to T, inertia is just μ. Along T itself, inertia is μ + 2α|T|². That's a real, checkable structure — it says a particle should be harder to accelerate along the \"timewave\" direction than perpendicular to it. This is the same shape as Lorentz-violating \"preferred direction\" theories (aether/bumblebee-type actions) already studied in the literature — which is a legitimate lineage to sit in, not a criticism.\n[L322]\n[L323] Step 3 — two things that stop you from going further, and they're not nitpicks:\n[L324]\n[L325] Sign of V. A standard mechanical Lagrangian is T − V (kinetic minus potential); the document writes \"+V_geom(λ).\" If that + is literal, this isn't producing time evolution via extremizing an action in the usual sense — it's closer to an energy/cost functional being minimized for a static embedding (more like elastic-rod or spline energy than particle dynamics). Those are both legitimate variational problems, but they're different problems with different Euler-Lagrange sign conventions and different physical interpretations of \"equations of motion.\" This has to be settled before anything downstream (mass generation, gravity, gauge structure) means what it's claimed to mean.\n[L326] What is H? If H is meant to be proper time along the worldline, the ½μ|λ'|² kinetic form is fine as written. If H is an arbitrary parameter (which \"superhelical expansion\" suggests — it sounds like an embedding parameter, not proper time), then a genuine relativistic worldline action needs to be reparametrization-invariant, which ½μ|λ'|² is not. The standard fix is L ∝ √(−ηλ'·λ'), or introducing an einbein field with a mass-shell constraint.             "They are not equivalent URLs because GitHub treats the pieces after `Satobloc/HsH` as part of its web-routing syntax, not simply as ordinary folders.\n\nI checked the repository: its default branch is `main`. The basic grammar is:\n\n`https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/tree/BRANCH/FOLDER`\n`https://github.com/OWNER/REPO/blob/BRANCH/FILE`\n\nSo `tree` means “show me a directory/tree,” `blob` means “show me a file,” and `main` tells GitHub which branch/version of the repository you mean.\n\n| URL | What GitHub interprets it as |\n|---|---|\n| `github.com/Satobloc/HsH/tree/` | **Incomplete `tree` route.** It says “show a tree…” but doesn't say which branch/ref. GitHub may redirect, complain, or resolve it strangely. Don't use this. |\n| `github.com/Satobloc/HsH/tree/main` | **Valid.** Root directory of the repository on branch `main`. This is effectively the normal file-browser view of HsH. |\n| `github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob` | **Incomplete `blob` route.** A blob URL requires a branch/ref **and a file path**. Don't use this. |\n| `github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/SABLE/CONTINUITY_CHECKPOINT.md` | **Valid file URL.** Open that specific Markdown file on `main`. |\n| `github.com/Satobloc/HsH/tree/main/WORKSPACES` | **Valid directory URL.** Open the `WORKSPACES` folder on `main`. |\n| `github.com/Satobloc/HsH/WORKSPACES` | **Not a repository-file path.** GitHub interprets `WORKSPACES` as a website route after the repository name, like `/issues`, `/pulls`, `/actions`, etc. Since `WORKSPACES` isn't one of those routes, it won't mean “open that folder.” |\n\nThe really counterintuitive part is the last one. On a normal web server you might expect:\n\n`HsH/WORKSPACES`\n\nto mean “folder WORKSPACES inside HsH.”\n\nGitHub doesn't work that way. Once you're inside a repository, repository contents have to go through a route indicating **what Git object/version you want**:\n\n```text\nHsH/tree/main/WORKSPACES\n    │    │       │\n    │    │       └── repo-relative folder\n    │    └────────── branch/ref\n    └─────────────── directory/tree viewer\n```\n\nAnd for a file:\n\n```text\nHsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/SABLE/CONTINUITY_CHECKPOINT.md\n    │    │       │\n    │    │       └── repo-relative file\n    │    └────────── branch/ref\n    └─────────────── file/blob viewer\n```\n\nFor our purposes, the safest mental shortcut is:\n\n**Repository root:** `https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH`\n\n**Any folder:** insert `/tree/main/` before its repository-relative path.\n\n**Any file:** insert `/blob/main/` before its repository-relative path.\n\nSo when I give you repo links going forward, I should generate them in exactly those canonical forms rather than casually constructing shortened GitHub paths. That is probably responsible for at least some of the “why did this link take me somewhere weird?” behavior we've been seeing."

\\n**Scope:** all scripts, GitHub Actions, bots, one-shot compute shims, local utilities, extraction jobs, indexing/tagging jobs, and automated write processes operating on any combination of **before file open/hash/index/sample operations**, not merely before publishing results.\\n- Quarantine-derived material must not leak into ordinary manifests, search indexes, logs, samples, filenames, or error reports beyond authorized minimal routing metadata.\\n- Direct theory construction/development remains sandbox-routed; infrastructure scripts must preserve sandbox/public/private distinctions rather than flatten them.\\n\\n## Write classes\\n\\n### A. Read-only / audit\\nSafest class. May inventory/hash/read permitted sources but makes no repo changes.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- exact source refs recorded;\\n- quarantine pruning before descent;\\n- outputs, if retained, are written separately as derived artifacts.\\n\\n### B. Derived/generated output\\nExamples: extracted images/text, manifests, Viewer catalogs, indexes, samples, generated reports.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- deterministic/rebuildable when feasible;\\n- write only inside declared generated/output paths;\\n- do not overwrite source artifacts;\\n- compare generated source coverage against current inputs before declaring success;\\n- publish from a fresh base;\\n- safe to regenerate rather than hand-merge when appropriate.\\n\\n### C. Append-only operational logs/handoffs\\nRequirements:\\n- re-fetch immediately before append;\\n- preserve existing entries exactly;\\n- if append cannot be made atomically or against current state, abort/retry rather than replace from a stale copy.\\n\\n### D. Destructive/renaming/migration jobs\\nExamples: delete, move, mass rename, directory restructuring, source rewriting.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- dry-run/default preview unless the operation is trivial and fully deterministic;\\n- pre-run manifest of affected paths and hashes;\\n- explicit source/destination collision handling;\\n- no overwrite-on-collision unless the workflow specifically proves identity and records the action;\\n- reversible mapping or backup/provenance sufficient to reconstruct prior location/content;\\n- post-run integrity check.\\n\\n## GitHub Contents API writes\\n\\nFor replacement updates, use the current blob SHA. This provides compare-and-swap behavior: stale writes should fail rather than silently clobber a newer version.\\n\\nRequired pattern:\\n1. fetch current target + SHA;\\n2. compute/reconcile update;\\n3. update with that SHA;\\n4. on stale-SHA failure, re-fetch and retry/reconcile; do not bypass the guard.\\n\\n## Git checkout / commit / push writes\\n\\nBefore publishing:\\n1. fetch current target branch;\\n2. rebase/reset/merge onto current branch as appropriate;\\n3. rerun any validation whose assumptions could have changed;\\n4. push without force;\\n5. if rejected, fetch again and retry non-destructively or stop for reconciliation.\\n\\n**Never force-push automated generated or semantic project updates to `main`.**\\n\\nOne-shot stage -> run -> cleanup GitHub Actions are allowed when their workflow is narrow, validated, and uses this fresh-base publish pattern.\\n\\n## Concurrency\\n\\nUse repository/workflow concurrency controls when two runs of the same job could overlap.\\n\\nConcurrency controls are a convenience, not the primary integrity mechanism: scripts must still tolerate another actor changing the repository while they run.\\n\\nFor long-running jobs:\\n- snapshot exact input commits at start;\\n- treat output as a product of those snapshots;\\n- before publishing semantic changes, reconcile against current target state;\\n- generated outputs may either publish snapshot-stamped results or rerun against newer input, but must not pretend stale input was current.\\n\\n## Cross-repo jobs\\n\\nA job reading multiple repositories must treat each repository as an independent versioned input.\\n\\nRecord the commit SHA for every repo. Do not use vague labels such as `latest` in retained run manifests.\\n\\nIf a combined output contains metadata/content from a private repository, default its destination to a private repository. Publication to a public repo requires an explicit safe-publication decision; do not infer one from the fact that other inputs were public.\\n\\n## Image / OCR / extraction jobs\\n\\nBecause extraction jobs may run simultaneously with archive work:\\n\\n- write only to dedicated derived-output trees;\\n- never modify the source PDF/image/binary;\\n- use source hash + relative path as identity, not filename alone;\\n- avoid a single shared temporary filename/path; use per-run temp directories;\\n- atomic finalization where possible: write temporary output, validate, then rename/move into final destination;\\n- if final destination already exists with the same source/tool identity, verify/reuse rather than blindly overwrite;\\n- if it differs, preserve both or route to reconciliation.\\n\\n## Temporary files\\n\\nTemporary/state files must be either:\\n- outside repository trees; or\\n- inside a clearly designated ignored/generated temp namespace.\\n\\nDo not leave generic names such as `output.json`, `temp.txt`, or `result.csv` at shared roots where concurrent jobs can overwrite one another.\\n\\n## Validation / post-run checks\\n\\nA script that writes should perform checks appropriate to its job, such as:\\n- expected outputs exist and are nonempty;\\n- JSON/YAML/CSV syntax validates;\\n- source count/coverage is plausible;\\n- output source IDs/hashes map back to actual inputs;\\n- no source files changed unexpectedly;\\n- quarantine exclusions remain absent;\\n- git diff contains only declared write scope;\\n- commit/push succeeded from a fresh base.\\n\\nUnexpected writes outside declared scope are a failure condition.\\n\\n## Run manifest / auditability\\n\\nFor substantial recurring or cross-repo jobs, prefer a compact machine-readable run record containing:\\n- run ID;\\n- start/end time;\\n- tool version;\\n- input repo SHAs;\\n- declared read/write scope;\\n- output hashes/counts;\\n- exclusions/quarantine-root counts without leaking quarantined content;\\n- success/failure status;\\n- published commit SHA(s).\\n\\nDo not record credentials/tokens.\\n\\n## Failure behavior\\n\\nOn ambiguity, collision, stale target, unknown source identity, or unexpected diff:\\n\\n**STOP / RETRY / ROUTE \\u2014 never guess and overwrite.**\\n\\nA failed run is preferable to silent data loss.\\n\\n## Worker / automation obligations\\n\\n- Workers may propose improvements, but Sable owns cross-lane workflow redesign and project-wide execution-safety policy unless Nathan says otherwise.\\n- Infrastructure QA should audit scripts/workflows for compliance opportunistically and after incidents.\\n- Newly written scripts should comply from first use.\\n- Existing scripts are grandfathered only temporarily; upgrade them when touched or when they become active collision risks.\\n- Repeated manual scripts should be promoted toward repo-native, reproducible workflows when practical.\\n\\n## Minimal compliance checklist\\n\\nBefore running a write-capable script, answer YES:\\n\\n- [ ] Exact read/write scope declared?\\n- [ ] Correct quarantine/sandbox routing enforced before file access?\\n- [ ] Source artifacts preserved?\\n- [ ] Fresh target state fetched immediately before semantic writes?\\n- [ ] CAS/current-SHA or fetch/rebase protection used?\\n- [ ] No force-push / blind overwrite?\\n- [ ] Concurrent temp/output names isolated?\\n- [ ] Private-derived output kept private by default?\\n- [ ] Outputs validated and unexpected diffs rejected?\\n- [ ] Enough run/source provenance retained to reproduce or audit the result?\\n\\nIf not, the script should be treated as needing a safety upgrade before unattended use.\\n\"}}"
